opus-5.5.text:
I think it covers a lot less than people intuitively assume. If you scroll through the internet, it feels like there are images and videos of everything, but the distribution is very skewed.

Think about what actually gets uploaded. People take photos and record videos of things they find worth sharing: travel, food, pets, events, products, movies, sports. That's the highlight reel of human life. The vast majority of what we actually see every day, the boring, continuous, first-person stream, almost never gets recorded. Opening a drawer, looking for your keys, reaching into the fridge, folding clothes, the way your hand approaches a cup before you grasp it. That's the bulk of our visual experience, and it's massively underrepresented.

There's also the viewpoint problem. Most internet images are third-person, taken by a photographer who framed the shot and chose a nice angle, usually at a moment when nothing is happening. Human vision is egocentric, continuous, and tightly coupled with action. Your eyes move because you're about to do something, and what you see next depends on what your hands just did. Internet video mostly lacks that closed loop between perception and action. Even egocentric datasets are still quite small compared with the total internet corpus, and they usually don't come with the action signals: forces, contacts, precise hand poses.

So if you ask how much of human visual experience the internet covers, I'd say it covers the semantic layer quite well. A model trained on internet data knows what a cup is, what a kitchen looks like, and roughly what people do in kitchens. That's why vision-language models are so good at recognition and description. But the physical, interactive layer, how objects deform, how much force it takes to open a stiff lid, what happens at the moment of contact, is very thinly covered. For a lot of the long-tail manipulation skills, it's close to zero.

That's why, from an embodied intelligence perspective, I don't think internet data alone gets you there. It's a great prior for understanding the world, but to act in the world you need data that is grounded in action. That's where things like simulation and synthetic data, plus a smaller amount of high-quality real-world robot data, become essential. You use the internet for breadth of semantics and generated or real interaction data for depth of physics and control. The gap between watching the world and acting in it is exactly where the hard problems are.

r001.rationale: The response says Internet data covers less than people assume and leaves everyday, first-person activity underrepresented, while describing semantic coverage as quite good. It does not clearly state that the overall coverage is only a tiny fraction of the full range of human visual experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, far less than people assume. If you think of everything a human sees over a lifetime, the images and videos on the Internet are a very biased, very thin slice of it.

Let me break that down. First, there's a selection bias. People take photos of things worth photographing: faces, food, landmarks, sunsets, their cat. Almost nobody uploads two hours of footage of themselves staring at the kitchen counter while washing dishes, or the inside of a drawer, or the floor as they walk. But that boring, ordinary visual stream is actually most of what a human visual system processes, and it's exactly what a robot has to deal with.

Second, there's the viewpoint problem. Internet images are overwhelmingly third-person, taken by a standing adult holding a phone at chest or eye height, framed nicely. Embodied visual experience is first-person, it's continuous, it's tied to your own body moving through space. Your head turns, your hands come into view, you get close to objects, you reach around them. That egocentric, interactive perspective is almost absent online, and the small amount that exists, like GoPro footage, is still curated.

Third, and I think this is the most important one, Internet data has no physical grounding. A video shows you what happened, but not what forces were applied, not the weight of the object, not what would have happened if you'd pushed a bit harder. Human visual experience is always coupled with action and consequence. You see because you're trying to do something. That coupling is the thing that makes vision useful for manipulation, and it's basically missing from web data.

So my rough assessment: the Internet covers the semantic layer very well. What is this object, what category, what's a typical scene. That's why large vision-language models feel so capable. But if you ask about the geometric, physical, interactive layer of human vision, the coverage is maybe a few percent, and it's not evenly distributed. The long tail of everyday states, like a half-open cabinet, a crumpled towel, a cup seen from six centimeters away, is where it falls apart.

That's why I don't think you can get to real embodied intelligence just by scaling Internet pretraining. You get a good prior, which matters, but you still need data generated by acting in the world, whether that's real robots or simulation. The Internet teaches a model what the world looks like. It doesn't teach it how the world responds.

r001.rationale: The response says Internet images and videos are a “very biased, very thin slice” of everything a person sees over a lifetime.

astra-6.text:
I think they cover a lot of what humans can see, but a much smaller fraction of how humans experience seeing. Internet images and videos are selected: people record things they find interesting, and the camera captures a particular viewpoint. Much of our everyday visual experience is mundane and continuous, so it never gets uploaded.

More importantly, human vision is interactive. We move our heads, walk around an object, pick it up, and see what changes. That connects vision to action and physical consequences. A video can show someone manipulating an object, but watching that video is different from choosing an action yourself and observing the result.

So I wouldn’t assign a precise percentage. The Internet provides enormous visual diversity, but it’s an incomplete sample of the experience of being an embodied agent in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says Internet media cover “a lot” of what humans can see and a “much smaller fraction” of how humans experience seeing, but it does not clearly state that they cover only a tiny fraction of the full range of visual experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Internet images and videos cover a broad range of what we see, but only a small part of how we experience seeing. They’re selected recordings: people tend to capture things that are interesting, beautiful, or unusual. Much of everyday visual experience is repetitive and never gets uploaded.

And our own vision is active. We move our eyes, turn our heads, approach an object, pick it up, and see what changes. That visual input is connected to touch, movement, and the consequences of our actions. A video can show someone interacting with the world, but watching that interaction isn’t the same as controlling it.

So I’d distinguish coverage of visual appearances from coverage of visual experience. The Internet gives us an enormous amount of the first. It’s much harder to say how much of the second it captures, and I wouldn’t put a reliable percentage on it.

r001.rationale: The response says Internet images and videos cover “only a small part” of how people experience seeing, matching the criterion’s claim that they capture only a tiny fraction of human visual experience.
